subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Building Monuments and Folding Solid Shapes

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Try to make a model Q1–Q5 + Discussion, p.1
tasks_in_class.description: Make a model of buildings using blocks; answer: what parts shown, why selected, what shapes, how similar/different, what if one piece removed.
Use nets from the end of the book to make models of prisms (triangular, square, hexagonal) and pyramids (triangular, square, pentagonal); identify common face shapes and meeting points.
Make shapes using straws and plasticine; fill in table of faces (F), corners (V), edges (E); identify F+V–E relationship.

time_bands.activity: Students handle wooden blocks and reconstruct a familiar monument shape, then discuss Try to make a model Q1–Q5 + Discussion, p.1 ("Make a model of buildings using blocks; answer: what parts shown..."), naming the block shapes they choose and comparing their models with a neighbour's.

Students fold pre-cut nets from the book to produce three prisms and two pyramids, working through Craft Q2, p.3 ("Use nets from the end of the book to make models of prisms..."). They place finished solids side-by-side and describe the face shapes common to all prisms and what is different about pyramids.

Using straws and plasticine, students build a cube and a triangular prism and then record F, V, and E for each in the table from Craft Q3, p.4 ("Make shapes using straws and plasticine; fill in table of faces (F)..."). Pairs share their counts aloud; the teacher guides the class to notice that F + V − E gives the same number for every solid built.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often miscount edges by counting vertices as edges — prompt them to run a finger along each edge, not tap each corner. The straws-and-plasticine task is open: students may build more than two solids if time allows, enriching the table. T-2 (Qutub Minar observation) and T-3 (sphere-like paper-strip craft) are light awareness tasks; use either as an optional extension or assign as home exploration.
materials: Pre-cut nets from end of textbook

section_titles: Faces, Edges, Corners — Observation and Classification
periods.activity_title: Sorting Solids by Faces, Edges, and Views

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Craft Q3 (sort by flat faces), p.4
tasks_in_class.description: Sort 3D shapes by number of flat faces and write names; determine if a 3D shape with 3 flat faces is possible.
Take a die; identify the face opposite to faces numbered 2, 3, and 4.
Look at three views of the same cube; deduce the colour of the face opposite to red, and opposite to yellow.
Write names of 3D shapes in Venn-diagram circles sorted by: all faces same vs. not same; straight vs. curved edges; triangular vs. rectangular faces (with both-category).

time_bands.activity: Students use the models built earlier (or textbook pictures) to sort solids by number of flat faces using Craft Q3 (sort by flat faces), p.4 ("Sort 3D shapes by number of flat faces and write names..."). The class debates whether any solid with exactly three flat faces is possible, sharing reasoning aloud.

Each pair takes a die and answers Let Us Observe Q1, p.5 ("Take a die; identify the face opposite to faces numbered 2, 3, and 4"). They then study a book diagram of three cube views for Let Us Observe Q3, p.5 ("Look at three views of the same cube; deduce the colour...") and record their deductions.

Students complete the three Venn-diagram sort tasks in Sorting 3D Shapes Q1–Q3, p.6–7 ("Write names of 3D shapes in Venn-diagram circles sorted by..."). Pairs compare diagrams and resolve disagreements; the teacher draws attention to solids that sit in the overlapping region of a Venn circle.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently place a cylinder in the 'all faces same' ring because its two circular faces look identical — prompt them to check every face of the solid, including curved surfaces. Let Us Observe Q2 (which faces share edges with face 1) and the border-colouring activity T-11 are parallel practice; note them as: additional practice: Let Us Observe Q2 and Let Us Observe (border activity), p.5. The Venn diagrams work best when students have a small set of physical or pictured solids to slide into categories rather than working from memory alone.
materials: Solid models from previous activity or textbook pictures

section_titles: Identifying 3D Shapes by Properties and Nets
periods.activity_title: Cube Towers, Dot-Paper Drawing, and Net Matching

tasks_in_class.description: Build models A, B, C, D with cubes from Jaadui Pitara Kit; count the cubes in each cube tower.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Drawing Cubes on a Triangular Dot Paper, p.8
tasks_in_class.description: Complete the partially drawn cubes on triangular dot paper.
Match six property-descriptions (faces, corners, edges) to the correct 3D shape names (a–f).
Match four nets (1–4) to the appropriate solids (a–d).

homework.description: Identify which of nets A, B, C, D can be folded to make the given solid.

time_bands.activity: Students use unit cubes from their kit to build structures A, B, C, and D shown in Build with Cubes A–D, p.7 ("Build models A, B, C, D with cubes from Jaadui Pitara Kit; count the cubes in each cube tower"). They record the cube count for each tower.

Students turn to the triangular dot paper in their books and complete the partially drawn cubes in Drawing Cubes on a Triangular Dot Paper, p.8 ("Complete the partially drawn cubes on triangular dot paper"). The teacher circulates, pointing out which edges should be drawn as dashed lines.

Students read each property description in Match the pictures Q1, p.8 ("Match six property-descriptions (faces, corners, edges) to the correct 3D shape names") and write the matching shape name. They cross-check with a partner.

Students study the four nets and four solids in Match the nets Q3, p.9 ("Match four nets (1–4) to the appropriate solids (a–d)"), sketching briefly how each net folds. Pairs discuss before writing final answers.

periods.teacher_notes: On triangular dot paper, students often draw the third visible face of a cube in the wrong direction — show one correct cube on the board and let students use it as a reference. For net matching, encourage students to trace the net with a finger, folding mentally at each edge, rather than guessing by shape count alone. T-16 (each-one-is-different discussion) and T-19 (pieces of net) are strong additional practice: Each one is different Q2, p.8 and Pieces of net Q5, p.9.

periods.activity_title: Making Angles with Straws and Folded Paper

tasks_in_class.description: Make a right angle with paper-folding; identify right angles in dot grid using a right-angle checker; find right angles in book, window, other objects.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (mark angles), p.10
tasks_in_class.description: Mark angles in five pictures (scissors, book corner, clock hands, etc.).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (draw right angles), p.12
tasks_in_class.description: Draw some right angles on the dot grid.

time_bands.activity: Each student takes two straws and opens them to form angles of different sizes at a central point, observing how the opening between arms changes. They look at yoga-posture pictures in the book and describe where angles appear, then move to marking angles in the five pictures of Let Us Do Q1 (mark angles), p.10 ("Mark angles in five pictures (scissors, book corner, clock hands, etc.)").

Students fold a square piece of paper in half and in half again to produce a corner, following Right Angles (fold paper), p.11 ("Make a right angle with paper-folding; identify right angles in dot grid using a right-angle checker..."). They use this paper corner as a checker to test angles on their desk — book corners, window frame, ruler edge — and mark which match the fold.

Students open their books to the dot grid and draw several angles of their own, then complete Let Us Do Q1 (draw right angles), p.12 ("Draw some right angles on the dot grid"). They verify each drawn angle against their paper-fold checker before recording.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the length of the arms with the size of the angle — use two straws of different lengths forming the same opening to address this directly. T-21 (classroom angles) is a quick paired discussion that enriches T-22; if the unit moves briskly, invite two or three students to call out classroom examples before beginning the paper-folding. The paper-fold checker should be kept by each student for the following angles work.

section_titles: Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes
periods.activity_title: Naming Angle Types and Testing Shape Rigidity

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Acute and Obtuse Angles (naming objects), p.12
tasks_in_class.description: Name classroom objects that have an acute angle; name objects that have an obtuse angle.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (draw acute/obtuse), p.13
tasks_in_class.description: Draw some acute angles on the top grid; draw a line to make an acute angle using each given line in the bottom grid. Repeat for obtuse angles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Shapes with Straws (triangle and rectangle), p.14
tasks_in_class.description: Make triangle and rectangle with straws and clay; push sides; trace shapes; observe rigidity and angle changes. Repeat for square and pentagon.
Examine given 4-sided shapes; discuss in what ways rectangle and square differ from the other shapes shown.

homework.book_ref: Let Us Do Q2 (colour-code angles), p.13
homework.description: Mark acute angles in red, right angles in green, and obtuse angles in blue in given figures.

time_bands.activity: Using the paper-fold right-angle checker made with folded paper, students look around the room and name objects whose corner is smaller than the checker (acute) and objects whose corner is larger (obtuse), responding to Acute and Obtuse Angles (naming objects), p.12 ("Name classroom objects that have an acute angle; name objects that have an obtuse angle"). A quick class list is built on the board.

Students complete Let Us Do Q1 (draw acute/obtuse), p.13 ("Draw some acute angles on the top grid; draw a line to make an acute angle using each given line..."), using their paper checker to verify each drawn angle is on the correct side of a right angle.

In pairs, students use straws and clay to build a triangle and a rectangle following Shapes with Straws (triangle and rectangle), p.14 ("Make triangle and rectangle with straws and clay; push sides; trace shapes; observe rigidity and angle changes..."). They push each shape gently from the side and observe which holds firm and which collapses, tracing both the original and the pushed form.

Students examine the 4-sided shapes shown in 4-sided shapes, p.15 ("Examine given 4-sided shapes; discuss in what ways rectangle and square differ from the other shapes shown") and share one observation aloud about what makes the rectangle and square special among four-sided shapes.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes call any sharp-looking angle 'acute' without comparing it to a right angle — reinforce the comparison: 'smaller than the fold, or bigger?' T-25 (angles in letter shapes) is a good additional practice: Acute and Obtuse Angles (letters), p.12. When pushing the straw rectangle, students may be surprised that the angles at corners change; name this observation explicitly so it connects to why triangles are used in bridges and roofs.

section_titles: Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes
periods.activity_title: Dot-Grid Polygons and Discovering Circle Properties

tasks_in_class.description: Draw several three- and four-sided shapes on the dot grid; circle shapes with one or more right angles; count shapes with 1, 2, 3, all right angles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Make (draw circle with scale), p.16
tasks_in_class.description: Mark a point A; draw many points equidistant from A; connect dots freehand to get a circle. Identify centre and radius.
Fold circular paper in half three different ways; measure each crease; note all creases are equal (diameters); measure radius; discuss relationship between radius and diameter.
Fold circular paper in half then half again to find that diameter is double the radius.

time_bands.activity: Students work on the dot grid for Dot grid (3- and 4-sided shapes), p.15 ("Draw several three- and four-sided shapes on the dot grid; circle shapes with one or more right angles; count shapes with 1, 2, 3, all right angles"), using their right-angle checker to test each corner. They count and record how many shapes they drew with all right angles and share one surprising shape with the class.

Students mark a central point on plain paper, then use a ruler to place many points each the same distance away, completing Let Us Make (draw circle with scale), p.16 ("Mark a point A; draw many points equidistant from A; connect dots freehand to get a circle"). They label the centre and draw one radius.

Students fold a circular paper cut-out in half along three different fold lines, following Amazing Circles Q1–Q5, p.17 ("Fold circular paper in half three different ways; measure each crease; note all creases are equal..."). They measure each crease with a thread and compare lengths, noting that every fold gives the same length.

Students fold the same circular paper in half once more, then fold again to halve the diameter, working through Let Us Do (diameter fold), p.18 ("Fold circular paper in half then half again to find that diameter is double the radius"). They measure the half-crease and record the relationship in words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may draw equidistant points but place them too far apart to produce a recognisable circle — encourage many closely-spaced points rather than just four or six. In Amazing Circles, students may measure imprecisely; accept near-equal readings and ask 'do you think they would be exactly equal if we could measure perfectly?' to build the conceptual claim. T-29 (pentagon rigidity and circle impossibility with straws) is additional practice for the straws investigation: Shapes with Straws (pentagon and circle), p.16.
materials: Circular paper cut-outs (at least 2 per student)

periods.activity_title: Compass Designs, Wheel Comparisons, and Shape Puzzles

tasks_in_class.description: Use a compass (with teacher help) to draw the three-step circle design; mark centre, radius, and diameter on the carpet design.
Observe wheels A, B, C, D; name the wheel with longest radius, shortest radius, longest diameter, shortest diameter.

Identify hidden shapes and write names; draw 2 lines to divide triangle into 1 square + 2 triangles; draw 2 lines to divide square into 3 triangles; draw cuts on shapes to get specified smaller shapes.
Sort 2D-shape cards into three groups by number of sides; draw sorted shapes and explain sorting.

time_bands.activity: With teacher guidance, students open a compass to a chosen distance and draw the three-step circle design described in Let Us Do (compass design), p.18 ("Use a compass (with teacher help) to draw the three-step circle design; mark centre, radius, and diameter on the carpet design"). They label the centre, one radius, and one diameter on their completed design.

Students study the four wheels in Look at the wheels, p.19 ("Observe wheels A, B, C, D; name the wheel with longest radius, shortest radius, longest diameter, shortest diameter") and write their answers, using what they know about diameter being double the radius to reason about which wheel is largest.

Students work individually on Puzzling Shapes Q1–Q4, p.19–20 ("Identify hidden shapes and write names; draw 2 lines to divide triangle into 1 square + 2 triangles; draw 2 lines to divide square into 3 triangles..."). The teacher invites one student to show their line-drawing solution under a document camera or on the board.

Students cut out or name the 2D-shape cards for Card Game, p.20 ("Sort 2D-shape cards into three groups by number of sides; draw sorted shapes and explain sorting"), arrange them in groups, and write a one-sentence justification for each group's label.

periods.teacher_notes: Students learning to use a compass often press too hard or let the pivot slip — show the pinch-grip technique and let students practise one circle before starting the design. In Puzzling Shapes, Q2 (dividing a triangle into one square and two triangles) surprises many students; allow trial-and-error drawing before sharing the solution. The connection between radius, diameter, and wheel size in Look at the wheels reinforces the folding discovery from the circles work, now in a pictorial context.
materials: 2D-shape cards (cut from book or pre-cut set)

section_titles: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
periods.activity_title: Spider Webs, Matchsticks, and Angle Hunts

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q1 (Squiggly spiders), p.21
tasks_in_class.description: Count triangles in triangular web; trace a path from A back to A without reusing a wall. Count rectangles in rectangular web; trace a path from A to B without reusing a wall.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q5 (model challenge), p.22
tasks_in_class.description: Make solid shape models using: (a) 12 straws + 8 clay balls; (b) 9 straws + 6 clay balls; (c) 15 straws + 10 clay balls; (d) 10 straws + 6 clay balls.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q6 (classify by angles), p.22
tasks_in_class.description: Classify shapes a–g into 3 angles / 4 angles / 5 angles groups; identify the relation between number of sides and number of angles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q8 (mark right angles), p.23
tasks_in_class.description: Mark right angles in each figure; write the number of right angles; identify shapes with only right angles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Try Q9 (identify angle types in shapes), p.23
tasks_in_class.description: Identify the shape that has: 2 right + 1 acute + 1 obtuse; 1 right + 2 obtuse + 1 acute; 2 obtuse + 2 acute; 4 right angles.

time_bands.activity: Students count triangles in the triangular spider-web and attempt to trace a path from A back to A without reusing a wall, then repeat for the rectangular web, working through Let Us Try Q1 (Squiggly spiders), p.21 ("Count triangles in triangular web; trace a path from A back to A without reusing a wall..."). Pairs compare traced paths and discuss whether a complete path is always possible.

Students use straws and clay balls to construct the four solids described in Let Us Try Q5 (model challenge), p.22 ("Make solid shape models using: (a) 12 straws + 8 clay balls; (b) 9 straws + 6 clay balls..."). They identify each solid's name and check their counts against the faces-edges-corners knowledge built across the chapter.

Students classify shapes a–g from Let Us Try Q6 (classify by angles), p.22 ("Classify shapes a–g into 3 angles / 4 angles / 5 angles groups; identify the relation between number of sides and number of angles"), then state in their own words the pattern they notice between the count of sides and count of angles.

Students mark right angles on each figure in Let Us Try Q8 (mark right angles), p.23 ("Mark right angles in each figure; write the number of right angles; identify shapes with only right angles"), then answer Let Us Try Q9 (identify angle types in shapes), p.23 ("Identify the shape that has: 2 right + 1 acute + 1 obtuse..."), using their paper-fold checker for uncertain angles.

periods.teacher_notes: The straw-and-clay-ball challenge (Q5) requires students to draw on the faces-edges-corners relationships explored throughout the chapter — prompt those who are stuck to recall how many edges and corners a cube has, then count straws and balls to check. The spider-web path tracing is an informal introduction to Eulerian paths; do not introduce the term, but celebrate students who notice that some paths seem impossible and invite them to guess why. Additional matchstick puzzles T-40, T-41, T-42, and shape-drawing T-45 are strong extensions: Let Us Try Q2–Q4 (p.21–22) and Let Us Try Q7 (p.23).

items.prompt: Look at the shapes of these blocks: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone. Which two block shapes would you choose to build a model of a tall tower with a pointed top? Draw the shapes you choose and write one sentence saying why you chose each one.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A cylinder or cuboid (for the tall body) and a cone (for the pointed top). Any two shapes whose function is justified — body block for height, cone for the pointed tip — are acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the shape of the block to the part of the building it will form.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may handle actual blocks and point; stretch: ask them to name a second way to build the same tower using different shapes.

exercise.book_ref: Try to make a model Q1–Q5 + Discussion, p.1
exercise.description: Make a model of buildings using blocks; answer: what parts shown, why selected, what shapes, how similar/different, what if one piece removed.

items.prompt: Riya folds a net and makes a solid. She says: 'All the faces that are not the top or bottom are rectangles, and the top and bottom faces are triangles.' What is the name of the solid she made? Write one reason for your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A triangular prism. Reason: a triangular prism has two triangular faces (top and bottom) and three rectangular faces on the sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the solid by matching its face shapes to the description given.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may look at a folded triangular prism model and count faces; stretch: ask what the net would look like — how many pieces and what shapes.

exercise.description: Use nets from the end of the book to make models of prisms (triangular, square, hexagonal) and pyramids (triangular, square, pentagonal); identify common face shapes and meeting points.

items.prompt: A tower is built by stacking unit cubes. The bottom layer has 3 cubes in a row. A second layer of 2 cubes sits on top, and a single cube sits on top of that. How many cubes are in the tower altogether?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the cubes in each layer and add the layers together.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Counts only the top two layers, missing the bottom layer.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Adds an extra cube, perhaps double-counting a shared cube between layers.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Counts 8, likely imagining a 2×2×2 cube rather than the described staircase tower.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use actual unit cubes to build the tower and count by touch; stretch: ask how many cubes would be needed to add one more layer of 4 at the bottom.

exercise.description: Build models A, B, C, D with cubes from Jaadui Pitara Kit; count the cubes in each cube tower.

items.prompt: Fold a square piece of paper in half, then fold it in half again. The corner of the folded paper is a right angle. Name two objects in your classroom where you can find a right angle. For each one, draw a small sketch and mark the right angle with a small square.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two of: corner of a book, corner of a window, corner of the blackboard, corner of a door frame, corner of a square tile — with a sketch and a small square marking the angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the folded-paper right-angle checker against the corner and check that it fits exactly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use their paper-fold checker to physically test each corner before drawing; stretch: name one object in the room that does NOT have a right angle and explain how they know.

exercise.description: Make a right angle with paper-folding; identify right angles in dot grid using a right-angle checker; find right angles in book, window, other objects.

items.section_title: Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes
items.prompt: Priya makes a rectangle with straws and clay and pushes one side gently. What does she observe?

options.label: A
options.text: The rectangle becomes a triangle.

options.label: B
options.text: The rectangle breaks apart into separate straws.

options.label: C
options.text: The rectangle leans and its angles change, but it still has four sides.

options.label: D
options.text: The rectangle stays exactly the same.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The rectangle leans and its angles change, but it still has four sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Pushing a four-sided straw shape changes the angles at the corners because quadrilaterals are not rigid.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses changing shape with changing the number of sides — a pushed rectangle does not lose a side.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Assumes all shapes are rigid like a triangle; does not account for the flexibility of four-sided straw frames.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the physical straw joints giving way with the mathematical observation; the clay joints flex rather than fully break.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may build and push an actual straw rectangle before answering; stretch: ask what would happen if a diagonal straw were added inside the rectangle.

exercise.book_ref: Shapes with Straws (triangle and rectangle), p.14
exercise.description: Make triangle and rectangle with straws and clay; push sides; trace shapes; observe rigidity and angle changes. Repeat for square and pentagon.

items.prompt: Arjun marks a centre point on paper, then carefully places 12 dots that are all the same distance from the centre. He joins the dots to draw a circle. What is the name we give to the distance from the centre to any dot on the circle? Write it and draw a circle with its centre and this distance labelled.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The distance is called the radius. The drawing should show a circle with a centre point and a line from the centre to the edge labelled 'radius'.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: All points on a circle are the same distance from the centre; that fixed distance is the radius.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may mark the centre and just label the dot they drew; stretch: draw two radii and label the line all the way across as the diameter.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Make (draw circle with scale), p.16
exercise.description: Mark a point A; draw many points equidistant from A; connect dots freehand to get a circle. Identify centre and radius.

items.prompt: Meena folds a circular piece of paper in half along three different fold lines and measures each crease. What does she find?

options.label: A
options.text: All three creases are equal in length and each passes through the centre.

options.label: B
options.text: Each crease is a different length.

options.label: C
options.text: The creases are equal but none of them passes through the centre.

options.label: D
options.text: The first crease is the longest and each new crease gets shorter.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: All three creases are equal in length and each passes through the centre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Every fold that halves a circle produces a diameter — all diameters are equal and all pass through the centre.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Thinks the fold direction changes the length; does not yet see that all diameters of one circle are equal.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Correctly observes equal lengths but misses that every diameter must pass through the centre.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Applies a shrinking pattern not supported by the folding; possibly confused with halving the paper further each time.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may fold a real paper circle and lay creases side by side to compare; stretch: measure one crease and the half-crease and state the relationship in numbers.

exercise.description: Fold circular paper in half three different ways; measure each crease; note all creases are equal (diameters); measure radius; discuss relationship between radius and diameter.

items.prompt: A student counts the faces, corners, and edges of a triangular prism and a square pyramid. She finds F = 5, V = 6, E = 9 for the prism and F = 5, V = 5, E = 8 for the pyramid. Compute F + V − E for each solid. What do you notice?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Triangular prism: 5 + 6 − 9 = 2. Square pyramid: 5 + 5 − 8 = 2. Both give the answer 2 — the relationship F + V − E = 2 holds for both solids.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Substitute the counted values into F + V − E and compute; compare the results across both solids.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may compute one solid at a time with teacher counting help; stretch: ask them to predict F + V − E for a cube (F=6, V=8, E=12) and check.

exercise.description: Make shapes using straws and plasticine; fill in table of faces (F), corners (V), edges (E); identify F+V–E relationship.

items.prompt: Can a 3D solid have exactly 3 flat faces?

options.label: A
options.text: No — a solid with 3 flat faces is not possible because any solid with flat faces needs at least 4.

options.label: B
options.text: No — because all flat-faced solids must have an even number of faces.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — a cone has exactly 3 flat faces.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — a triangular prism has exactly 3 flat faces.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No — a solid with exactly 3 flat faces is not possible; all flat-faced polyhedra have at least 4 faces (the tetrahedron has 4).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sort known solids by face count; the smallest count found among flat-faced solids is 4 (tetrahedron), so 3 is impossible.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Misremembers the face count of a triangular prism, which has 5 faces (2 triangular + 3 rectangular).
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses a cone's curved surface with a flat face; a cone has one circular flat face and one curved surface.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Applies an invented rule about even numbers; even-number is not the constraint — minimum 4 is.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may list all solids they know and count faces one by one; stretch: ask them to draw the solid with the fewest flat faces and name it.

exercise.book_ref: Craft Q3 (sort by flat faces), p.4
exercise.description: Sort 3D shapes by number of flat faces and write names; determine if a 3D shape with 3 flat faces is possible.

items.section_title: Faces, Edges, Corners — Observation and Classification
items.prompt: A cube has six faces. You are told that the face coloured red is opposite the face coloured blue, and the face coloured green is opposite the face coloured yellow. Name the colour of the face that is opposite the white face. Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Orange (or whatever the sixth colour is). A cube has 6 faces forming 3 opposite pairs. Red–blue and green–yellow account for 4 faces; the remaining two faces (white and the sixth colour) must be opposite each other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A cube's 6 faces form 3 opposite pairs; subtract the 2 named pairs to find the third pair.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a real die and look at it directly; stretch: describe the full arrangement of all 6 faces in their own words.

exercise.description: Look at three views of the same cube; deduce the colour of the face opposite to red, and opposite to yellow.

items.section_title: Faces, Edges, Corners — Observation and Classification
items.prompt:
Sort the following shapes into the correct column of the table: sphere, cube, cylinder, cone, triangular prism.

Write each shape name under the correct heading.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Only straight edges | Has at least one curved edge |
|---|---|
| | |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Only straight edges: cube, triangular prism. Has at least one curved edge: sphere, cylinder, cone.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Examine each solid and decide whether any of its edges are curved; place it in the matching column.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may handle a model or picture of each solid and run a finger along its edges; stretch: add a square pyramid to the table and justify its placement.

exercise.description: Write names of 3D shapes in Venn-diagram circles sorted by: all faces same vs. not same; straight vs. curved edges; triangular vs. rectangular faces (with both-category).

items.section_title: Identifying 3D Shapes by Properties and Nets
items.prompt: Which 3D shape has exactly 6 faces, 8 corners, and 12 edges, with all faces rectangular?

options.label: A
options.text: Cube

options.label: B
options.text: Cuboid

options.label: C
options.text: Square pyramid

options.label: D
options.text: Triangular prism

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cuboid.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the given counts (6 faces, 8 corners, 12 edges, all rectangular) to the properties of each named solid.

what_each_option_reveals.A: A cube has 6 faces, 8 corners, and 12 edges, but all its faces are squares (a special rectangle); students may not distinguish cube from cuboid on the 'all rectangular' clue.
what_each_option_reveals.D: A triangular prism has 5 faces, 6 corners, and 9 edges — different counts on all three attributes.
what_each_option_reveals.C: A square pyramid has 5 faces, 5 corners, and 8 edges, and its faces are not all rectangular.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a table of face/corner/edge counts from earlier work to look up the answer; stretch: write the counts for a cube and explain how cube and cuboid are alike and different.

exercise.description: Match six property-descriptions (faces, corners, edges) to the correct 3D shape names (a–f).

items.section_title: Identifying 3D Shapes by Properties and Nets
items.prompt: A net is made of two circles and one rectangle joined along its long edges. Which solid does this net make?

options.label: A
options.text: Cone

options.label: B
options.text: Cuboid

options.label: C
options.text: Cylinder

options.label: D
options.text: Triangular prism

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cylinder.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A cylinder's net has one rectangular curved surface that rolls into the side, plus two circular faces for the top and bottom.

what_each_option_reveals.A: A cone's net has one circle and one sector (fan-shape), not two circles and a rectangle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: A cuboid's net has six rectangles, not two circles.
what_each_option_reveals.D: A triangular prism's net has two triangles and three rectangles, not circles.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may fold a real cylinder net; stretch: describe or sketch what a cone's net looks like instead.

exercise.description: Match four nets (1–4) to the appropriate solids (a–d).

items.prompt: The minute hand and hour hand of a clock form an angle. At 3 o'clock, the two hands are at a right angle. If the minute hand moves forward a little so the angle between the hands becomes smaller than a right angle, what type of angle is it now?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute angle

options.label: B
options.text: Obtuse angle

options.label: C
options.text: Right angle

options.label: D
options.text: Straight angle

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Acute angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: An angle smaller than a right angle is called an acute angle.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses smaller-than-right with larger-than-right; obtuse is greater than a right angle.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Does not update the angle type after the movement — the angle was right before moving, not after.
what_each_option_reveals.D: A straight angle is a flat line (two right angles combined), much larger than a right angle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a folded paper right-angle checker alongside a clock picture; stretch: name the time when clock hands form an obtuse angle and justify.

exercise.book_ref: Acute and Obtuse Angles (naming objects), p.12
exercise.description: Name classroom objects that have an acute angle; name objects that have an obtuse angle.

items.section_title: Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes
items.prompt: Look at the four-sided shapes below and answer: What do rectangles and squares have that the other four-sided shapes do not always have? Write one sentence.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Shape | All angles right angles? |
|---|---|
| Rectangle | Yes |
| Square | Yes |
| Parallelogram | No |
| Irregular quadrilateral | No |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rectangles and squares have all four angles as right angles, while the other four-sided shapes do not always have right angles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the angle type at each corner of each shape; rectangles and squares are the four-sided shapes where every corner is a right angle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a right-angle checker on printed shapes; stretch: name one more property that square has that rectangle does not necessarily have.

exercise.description: Examine given 4-sided shapes; discuss in what ways rectangle and square differ from the other shapes shown.

items.prompt: Siya folds a circular paper in half. The crease is 10 cm long. She then folds the same paper in half again. How long is the new crease? Write your answer and explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The new crease is 10 cm long (it is still a diameter of the same circle). Every fold that halves the circle produces a crease that passes through the centre and has the same length as every other diameter.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Any fold that halves a circle produces a diameter; all diameters of the same circle are equal.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may physically fold a paper circle and measure both creases; stretch: what is the radius of this circle, and how do you know?

exercise.description: Fold circular paper in half then half again to find that diameter is double the radius.

items.prompt: Four circular wheels are drawn. Wheel P has a radius of 6 cm, Wheel Q has a radius of 4 cm, Wheel R has a diameter of 14 cm, and Wheel S has a diameter of 8 cm. Which wheel has the longest diameter?

options.label: A
options.text: Wheel P

options.label: B
options.text: Wheel Q

options.label: C
options.text: Wheel R

options.label: D
options.text: Wheel S

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Wheel R, with a diameter of 14 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert all radii to diameters (diameter = 2 × radius) then compare all four diameters: P=12, Q=8, R=14, S=8.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Wheel P has radius 6 cm, giving diameter 12 cm — less than Wheel R's 14 cm; student may have compared radii without doubling.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Wheel Q has the smallest radius (4 cm) and therefore the smallest diameter (8 cm); student may have picked the first wheel listed.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Wheel S has diameter 8 cm — equal to Wheel Q and smaller than R; student may not have converted Wheel P and R correctly.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may write out the diameter for each wheel before comparing; stretch: rank all four wheels from shortest to longest diameter.

exercise.description: Observe wheels A, B, C, D; name the wheel with longest radius, shortest radius, longest diameter, shortest diameter.

items.prompt: A large square is divided into smaller shapes by drawing two straight lines inside it. Name two different ways you could draw two lines to create only triangles inside the square. How many triangles does each way produce?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One diagonal divides the square into 2 triangles; drawing both diagonals divides it into 4 triangles. (Accept any valid description of two-line divisions that produce only triangles.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw lines from corner to corner (diagonals) and count the triangular regions formed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw the square on dot paper and draw lines until they see triangles; stretch: can they find a way to divide the square into exactly 3 triangles with two lines?

exercise.description: Identify hidden shapes and write names; draw 2 lines to divide triangle into 1 square + 2 triangles; draw 2 lines to divide square into 3 triangles; draw cuts on shapes to get specified smaller shapes.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: A spider web is shaped like a triangle with two more lines drawn inside, making 4 smaller triangles in total. How many triangles can you count in the web altogether, including the big outer triangle and all the smaller ones? Write the number and explain how you counted.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Counting varies by the exact arrangement, but in a triangle divided into 4 smaller triangles (one large, with a row of 3 small ones), the total is typically 4 small + 1 large = 5 triangles. Accept any count with a clear, correct explanation of how overlapping regions were included.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the smallest triangles first, then count each group of smaller triangles that together form a larger triangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may colour each triangle a different colour as they count; stretch: draw a similar web with one more inner line and predict the new triangle count.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q1 (Squiggly spiders), p.21
exercise.description: Count triangles in triangular web; trace a path from A back to A without reusing a wall. Count rectangles in rectangular web; trace a path from A to B without reusing a wall.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: A shape has 5 sides. How many angles does it have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 angles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The number of angles in any polygon equals the number of its sides; a 5-sided shape has 5 angles.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Off by one; student may be subtracting 1 from the side count, perhaps thinking of diagonals.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Off by one in the other direction; student may be adding 1, perhaps confusing sides with corners of a different shape.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Doubles the count; student may be thinking of both sides and angles separately and adding them.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw a pentagon and mark each angle as they count; stretch: state how many angles a shape with 8 sides would have, without drawing it.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q6 (classify by angles), p.22
exercise.description: Classify shapes a–g into 3 angles / 4 angles / 5 angles groups; identify the relation between number of sides and number of angles.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: Which description matches a shape that has 2 right angles, 1 acute angle, and 1 obtuse angle?

options.label: A
options.text: A four-sided shape (quadrilateral) with a mix of angle types

options.label: B
options.text: A shape with three sides and three angles, all acute

options.label: C
options.text: A square

options.label: D
options.text: A triangle with one right angle

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A four-sided shape (quadrilateral) with a mix of angle types.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the total angles described (2 + 1 + 1 = 4); a shape with 4 angles is a four-sided shape, and the mix of types rules out a square.

what_each_option_reveals.D: A triangle has only 3 angles; the description has 4 angles total, so a triangle cannot fit.
what_each_option_reveals.C: A square has 4 right angles; this shape has only 2 right angles plus acute and obtuse ones.
what_each_option_reveals.B: A shape with all acute angles cannot contain right or obtuse angles; also a triangle has only 3 angles.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may count the angles described first (2+1+1=4) before looking at the options; stretch: draw a four-sided shape that fits the description and label each angle type.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q9 (identify angle types in shapes), p.23
exercise.description: Identify the shape that has: 2 right + 1 acute + 1 obtuse; 1 right + 2 obtuse + 1 acute; 2 obtuse + 2 acute; 4 right angles.

items.prompt: On the triangular dot paper below, a cube has been started for you — two edges are already drawn. Complete the drawing of the cube by adding all the remaining edges. Remember to show the three visible faces.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A completed cube on triangular dot paper showing three visible parallelogram faces meeting at a top-front corner, with dashed or solid lines for all 12 edges. The drawing should look like a three-faced 3D cube.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: On triangular dot paper, each cube edge follows one of the three grid directions; draw the remaining 10 edges in the matching directions.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a reference cube drawing from the textbook to count and copy lines; stretch: draw a tower of two cubes stacked on the same dot paper.

exercise.book_ref: Drawing Cubes on a Triangular Dot Paper, p.8
exercise.description: Complete the partially drawn cubes on triangular dot paper.

items.prompt: A picture shows four things: a pair of open scissors, a folded book lying flat, the corner of a square tile, and a clock showing 3 o'clock. Which of these shows an angle that is NOT a right angle?

options.label: A
options.text: A folded book lying flat

options.label: B
options.text: None — all four show right angles

options.label: C
options.text: The clock at 3 o'clock

options.label: D
options.text: The corner of a square tile

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A folded book lying flat — the book's spine makes a straight (180-degree) angle, not a right angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test each example against the right-angle checker; a book folded completely flat opens to a straight line, which is wider than a right angle.

what_each_option_reveals.D: A square tile corner is exactly a right angle; choosing this shows confusion between flat and right.
what_each_option_reveals.C: A clock at 3 o'clock shows the two hands at 90 degrees — a right angle; choosing this shows the student has not visualised the clock correctly.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Accepting all four as right angles shows the student has not distinguished a straight angle (flat book) from a right angle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a paper-fold checker and physically place it against each example; stretch: name the type of angle a fully open flat book makes.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (mark angles), p.10
exercise.description: Mark angles in five pictures (scissors, book corner, clock hands, etc.).

items.prompt: On the dot grid below, draw three different right angles. Mark each one with a small square in the corner to show it is a right angle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three different right-angle drawings on the dot grid, each with arms going along grid lines and a small square at the vertex. The arms may point in any of the four grid directions as long as they are perpendicular.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: On a dot grid, draw one arm along a horizontal grid line and the other along a vertical grid line; these are always perpendicular and form a right angle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may trace the corner of their textbook onto the dot grid as a starting shape; stretch: draw a right angle whose arms are diagonal on the dot grid (using dots diagonally).

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (draw right angles), p.12
exercise.description: Draw some right angles on the dot grid.

items.prompt: A dot-grid has a line drawn from one dot going to the right. You draw another line from the same starting dot so that the angle between the two lines is acute. Which direction should your new line go?

options.label: A
options.text: Down and to the left, making a wide opening between the lines

options.label: B
options.text: Slightly upward and to the right, making a small opening between the lines

options.label: C
options.text: Straight to the left, making a straight line with the first line

options.label: D
options.text: Straight up, making a right angle with the first line

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Slightly upward and to the right, making a small opening between the lines.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle; keep the second line close to the first so the opening between them is narrow.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Straight up makes a right angle, not an acute angle — the student knows about right angles but does not relate acute to being smaller.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Straight left makes a straight angle (flat line), which is much larger than a right angle.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Down and to the left creates a wide, obtuse or reflex angle — larger than a right angle, the opposite of acute.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use two straws to make the angle and compare it to their paper-fold right-angle checker; stretch: draw both an acute and an obtuse angle from the same starting line and label them.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 (draw acute/obtuse), p.13
exercise.description: Draw some acute angles on the top grid; draw a line to make an acute angle using each given line in the bottom grid. Repeat for obtuse angles.

items.section_title: Shapes with Straws — Rigidity and 2D Shapes
items.prompt: On the dot grid below, draw two different three-sided shapes and two different four-sided shapes. Circle any shape that has at least one right angle. Write how many of your shapes have a right angle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Four shapes drawn (2 triangles and 2 quadrilaterals of any form). Right angles identified correctly using a right-angle checker. The count written matches the number circled.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw shapes on the dot grid using the grid points; test each corner with a right-angle checker to decide whether to circle the shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may trace a textbook shape onto the dot grid as one of their shapes; stretch: draw a four-sided shape with exactly two right angles and one with no right angles.

exercise.description: Draw several three- and four-sided shapes on the dot grid; circle shapes with one or more right angles; count shapes with 1, 2, 3, all right angles.

items.prompt: Using a compass, draw a circle with any radius you choose. On your circle, mark the centre with a dot, draw one radius and label it 'radius', then draw a diameter and label it 'diameter'.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A circle drawn with a compass. A dot at the centre. A line from the centre to the circumference labelled 'radius'. A line passing through the centre from one side of the circle to the other, labelled 'diameter'.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Open the compass to the chosen radius, place the pivot at the centre, and draw; then mark centre, draw radius and diameter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a traced circular object and mark the centre by folding; stretch: measure the radius and diameter and write the relationship as a number sentence.

exercise.description: Use a compass (with teacher help) to draw the three-step circle design; mark centre, radius, and diameter on the carpet design.

items.prompt: Below are six 2D shapes: triangle, square, rectangle, pentagon, hexagon, circle. Sort them into three groups by the number of sides they have. Write the group heading and list the shapes under each heading.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 sides: triangle. 4 sides: square, rectangle. More than 4 sides: pentagon (5), hexagon (6). Circle: 0 sides (accept as a separate group or note that a circle has no straight sides).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the straight sides of each shape and place it under the matching number heading.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw each shape and trace its sides with a finger while counting; stretch: add two more shapes of their own to any group and name them.

exercise.description: Sort 2D-shape cards into three groups by number of sides; draw sorted shapes and explain sorting.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: Look at the four figures below (a square, a rectangle, a right-angled triangle, and a pentagon). For each figure, mark all the right angles with a small square and write the total number of right angles in that figure.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Figure | Number of right angles |
|---|---|
| Square | |
| Rectangle | |
| Right-angled triangle | |
| Pentagon (regular) | |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Square: 4. Rectangle: 4. Right-angled triangle: 1. Pentagon (regular): 0.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use a right-angle checker at each corner of each figure and count every corner where it fits exactly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may use a folded-paper right-angle checker physically on a drawn or printed figure; stretch: name a shape with exactly 2 right angles and draw it.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q8 (mark right angles), p.23
exercise.description: Mark right angles in each figure; write the number of right angles; identify shapes with only right angles.

items.section_title: Let Us Try — Reasoning and Puzzle Tasks
items.prompt: A solid shape is built using straws as edges and clay balls as corners. The solid has 6 clay balls and 9 straws. Use what you know about faces, edges, and corners of 3D shapes to work out: how many flat faces does this solid have? Write your answer as a number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 faces. Using F + V − E = 2: F + 6 − 9 = 2, so F = 2 + 9 − 6 = 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply F + V − E = 2 with V = 6 and E = 9 to find F = 5.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may build the shape with actual straws and clay balls and count the faces directly; stretch: name the solid that has 6 clay balls, 9 straws, and 5 faces.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Try Q5 (model challenge), p.22
exercise.description: Make solid shape models using: (a) 12 straws + 8 clay balls; (b) 9 straws + 6 clay balls; (c) 15 straws + 10 clay balls; (d) 10 straws + 6 clay balls.
